title: Newsweek Reported Trump Hotels Paid for a 1998 Cuba Business Trip
description_short: Newsweek reported Trump Hotels paid $68,551.88 for a 1998 Cuba business trip; it described a possible embargo violation, not a government fine.
description_medium: Newsweek reported in 2016 that Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts paid a consulting firm $68,551.88 for expenses tied to a 1998 trip to Cuba to explore business opportunities. The report said an OFAC license was required and described the spending as potentially unlawful. It did not report an official fine or establish Donald Trump’s personal role.
description_long: Newsweek reported in September 2016 that Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts paid Seven Arrows Investment and Development Corp. $68,551.88 for expenses connected to a 1998 trip to Cuba to explore business opportunities. The story, citing company records and interviews with former executives, said the consulting firm later invoiced the company for the trip. Trade experts told Newsweek that using U.S. company money for Cuba activity without an Office of Foreign Assets Control license could have violated the embargo. Newsweek described a potential violation, not a government finding. The report did not say Treasury or OFAC fined Trump Hotels, and the cited material identifies no enforcement action or settlement. It also does not establish that Donald Trump arranged or personally took part in the trip. This account concerns a reported payment by the Trump hotel-casino company and the legal concern experts raised about it.

title: 2019 U.S.–Honduras Asylum Agreement Set a Framework for Third-Country Transfers
description_short: The 2019 U.S.–Honduras agreement allowed certain asylum seekers to be transferred to Honduras, subject to exceptions.
description_medium: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 25, 2019. Its text provided for transferring certain non-Honduran nationals who arrived at or between U.S. ports of entry and requested protection to pursue claims in Honduras. It excluded Honduran nationals, unaccompanied minors, and specified visa holders or travelers who did not need a Honduran visa. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020; it does not establish how many transfers occurred or the protections available in practice.
description_long: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 25, 2019. It provided a framework for transferring certain non-Honduran nationals who arrived at or between U.S. ports of entry and requested protection so they could seek protection in Honduras. The text excluded Honduran nationals and unaccompanied children, and included exceptions for some valid U.S. visa holders and travelers not required to obtain a Honduran visa. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020. It called on the governments to develop operating procedures and an implementation plan covering transfers and the receiving system’s capacity in Honduras. The Department of Homeland Security described the arrangement as applying to certain third-country nationals, rather than automatically covering every asylum seeker. The agreement defines a transfer process but does not report how many people were transferred or the outcomes of individual claims. Its provisions alone do not establish how protections operated in practice.

Donald Trump’s Schedule 13D, filed April 1, reported beneficial ownership of 78,750,000 shares, approximately 57.6 percent of the shares outstanding on March 25. These filings establish the merger date and Trump’s reported share count and percentage. The SEC records establish the transaction and reported ownership, not a financial-misconduct conclusion.
